The authors write that even the single most over-represented name in each cluster (Dogwalker OG, 100% in Cluster I; Blue Dream, 88.5% in Cluster II; Dutch Treat, 85.9% in Cluster III) is not perfectly associated with one chemotype, and that products under each name vary within the cluster. Measurements came from six laboratories using methods that may not be standardized (cannabinoids by HPLC with diode-array or UV detection; terpenes by GC-FID or GC-MS, reported in % weight, ppm or mg/g); the authors cannot tell whether regional differences reflect real variation or laboratory methods; testing is not standardized nationally, so the main analyses used only compounds measured by every laboratory. Caveats listed by the authors: pooled data from different states, no genotype or growing conditions, compounds not measured everywhere, different state rules, hemp not included.

Leafly allowed the corresponding author (N.J.) professional time for the project but gave no other funding and, by the statement, had no role in design, laboratory data collection and analysis, the decision to publish or the manuscript; N.J. is employed by Leafly Holdings; D.V. founded the non-profit Agricultural Genomics Foundation and owns CGRI, LLC. N.J. is the only author listed for conceptualization, investigation, supervision and validation, and is also listed for data curation, methodology, project administration and writing.

Terpenes are described as responsible for cannabis's odours; consumers often believe Indica-labelled products are sedating and Sativa-labelled ones energizing; whether different cannabinoid and terpene ratios consistently give different subjective effects is stated to be unknown. No effects were measured. The Discussion concludes that the Indica/Hybrid/Sativa system does not reliably distinguish samples by chemical content, that it is therefore highly unlikely to indicate systematically different effects, and that strain names may be better markers of chemistry than the categories but are far from ideal.

Ten coffee shops in Amsterdam, Utrecht, Groningen and Maastricht, each visited twice about two months apart; 1 g each of Amnesia (described as a Sativa-dominant type) and White Widow (an Indica-dominant type), chosen because both were generally available at all locations throughout the year; 5 of 40 planned purchases unavailable, leaving 18 Amnesia and 17 White Widow samples; 28 compounds present at a mean of at least 0.5 mg/g, quantified by GC-FID in one laboratory.

Three of the samples bought had the chemical fingerprint of the other cultivar; the authors assumed mix-ups at the coffee shop and excluded them, conceding that they might be genuine specimens, which would widen the variation within each cultivar (the text and the figure legend disagree on which way the mix-ups went). Relative standard deviations above 25% were found for 14 compounds across purchases (by the editors' count of Table 1, 14 compound-and-cultivar pairs, 13 distinct compounds, beta-caryophyllene exceeding 25% in both cultivars, reading the misaligned gamma-selinene row, whose 34.6 is printed in Amnesia's SD column, as Amnesia's RSD). The dotted group outlines in Fig 2 were drawn by the authors and signify no test.

Popular descriptions of Sativa effects (uplifting, energetic) and Indica effects (body relaxation, sleep) are summarized from a popular book, and the authors state it has not been properly confirmed whether such descriptions relate to the Indica-Sativa distinction or to any chemical classification; no effects were measured. The pharmacy varieties came from the official Dutch grower, Bedrocan BV; each cultivar's Sativa or Indica background was taken from a seed company's website (Sensi Seed Bank); the first author has been employed by Bedrocan BV as head of research and development since February 2011. No test statistic or p value is reported for any comparison: differences called significant in the text come without a named test, and Bedrocan is called significantly different only because it lies outside the PCA plot's 95% confidence ellipse.

evidence_set: 130 family members seeking help about the drinking of someone living with them, mostly recruited through local news media in Albuquerque; included if living with a close relative, spouse or partner described as meeting DSM-III-R criteria for alcohol abuse or dependence, who refused treatment, with contact on at least 40% of the past 90 days; excluded if the relative had domestic violence or criminal assault in the past 2 years, a history of severe violence or an illicit drug problem more severe than the alcohol problem, or if there was any evidence of crack cocaine or injecting drug use (the paper does not say whose). 118 (91%) women; spouses 59%, parents 30%, partners 8%; assigned to Al-Anon facilitation (45), Johnson Institute intervention (40) or CRAFT (45); all retained in the analyses (intention to treat).

evidence_set: Withdrawal symptoms can ensue after 4–6 weeks of use but only in about 15–30% of patients, cited to ref. 124, the author's own 1998 paper on withdrawal reactions after stopping hypnotics in patients with insomnia (CNS Drugs); why some people stop after years of use without trouble while others suffer severely is unclear; dose reduction as well as stopping can bring symptoms. Rebound, the original symptoms returning more intensely for a time, is likely when stopping hypnotic benzodiazepines, especially short-acting ones, even after only a few days or nights of use.

More serious or life-threatening symptoms may occasionally occur; many are reported anecdotally, few case series exist, and their status remains controversial. Table 4 (severe symptoms that may accompany abrupt discontinuation but may occur despite slow tapering; sourced to a University of Newcastle guide, ref. 120, and the author's 1984 monograph with Petursson, ref. 125, with the depression entry cited to a report of four cases by the author and a colleague, ref. 276) lists delirium tremens, convulsions and status epilepticus which may end in death, catatonia which may result in death, depression (often severe) with possible suicidal ideation, self-harm, suicidal ideation, suicide and attempted suicide, homicidal thoughts, violence, organic brain syndrome, psychosis, mania, delusions and confusion, with no frequencies. Whether withdrawal occurs relates to high dosage and long-term treatment, but its severity less closely (ref. 122); severe withdrawal may still occur despite slow withdrawal over several months or even years (ref. 123).
Dependence and withdrawal, 8th and 10th paragraphs (p. 2092); Table 4 (p. 2093); References, refs. 120 and 125 (p. 2105) and ref. 276 (p. 2109)

Substituting a long-acting benzodiazepine before tapering has little evidence of efficacy, and the rate of taper rests on prescribers' clinical experience rather than good empirical evidence; with slow tapering about two-thirds of patients stop completely (no citation). Summary: withdrawal can be hazardous, with fits, psychosis and depression, and the outcome is usually favourable with tapered withdrawal, with a worse prognosis in elderly people. In high-dose use, as with low-dose dependence, tolerance sets in rapidly and withdrawal syndromes, sometimes severe with fits and psychotic reactions, can follow attempted stopping. No study comparing abrupt with gradual stopping for seizures is cited.
